_about: A small DEMO guideline corpus for the Week 2 evidence retriever. Written for this project as plain-language summaries of widely-taught primary-care principles. It is teaching material for a demo, NOT clinical guidance, and carries no patient data. Every chunk is labelled so retrieved evidence is always rendered as guideline text, never as a fact about the patient.

chunks.title: Penicillin allergy
chunks.text: Amoxicillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic. A documented penicillin allergy is therefore a contraindication to amoxicillin, and prescribing it to a patient with that allergy risks the same reaction. Where the recorded reaction is a mild rash, a clinician may still judge the risk acceptable; where it is anaphylaxis, the class should be avoided outright.

chunks.title: Penicillin allergy
chunks.text: When a penicillin-class antibiotic is contraindicated, commonly taught alternatives for routine outpatient infections include macrolides such as azithromycin and, for some indications, doxycycline. The right choice depends on the infection being treated and on local resistance patterns.

chunks.title: Penicillin allergy
chunks.text: A large share of recorded penicillin allergies turn out, on review, not to be true allergies. Because of this, an allergy label is worth confirming rather than assuming, and the recorded reaction matters as much as the label itself. Until it is reviewed, the recorded allergy stands.

chunks.title: Potassium
chunks.text: Serum potassium is commonly reported with a reference range of roughly 3.5 to 5.1 mmol/L. A result above the upper limit is termed hyperkalaemia and a result below the lower limit hypokalaemia. Reference ranges vary between laboratories, so the range printed on the report takes precedence.

chunks.title: Potassium
chunks.text: A mildly raised potassium result is often rechecked before action is taken, because a haemolysed sample can raise the measured value artefactually. Markedly raised potassium is treated as urgent because of its effect on cardiac rhythm.

chunks.title: Potassium
chunks.text: Several common medicines raise serum potassium, including ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, angiotensin receptor blockers, and potassium-sparing diuretics. When potassium is rising in a patient on these agents, the medication list is a routine place to look.

chunks.title: Hypertension
chunks.text: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor used in hypertension and in some kidney and heart conditions. Renal function and serum potassium are usually checked before starting and after dose changes, because the drug can raise potassium and affect kidney function.

chunks.title: Hypertension
chunks.text: Blood pressure control is assessed over repeated readings rather than a single measurement, since a single high reading may reflect the setting rather than the patient. Home readings are often used alongside clinic readings.

chunks.title: Hypertension
chunks.text: A persistent dry cough is a recognised side effect of ACE inhibitors and is a common reason for switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker. A new dry cough in a patient recently started on lisinopril is worth connecting to the medication rather than investigated in isolation.

chunks.title: Diabetes
chunks.text: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the preceding two to three months. It is commonly reported in mmol/mol or as a percentage, and is used both to diagnose and to monitor diabetes. Because it is an average, a single value does not describe day-to-day variability.

chunks.title: Diabetes
chunks.text: HbA1c is typically rechecked every three to six months while treatment is being adjusted, and less often once results are stable at target. Checking sooner than about three months is of limited value because the measure lags behind change.

chunks.title: Diabetes
chunks.text: Patients with diabetes are usually monitored for kidney involvement with periodic urine albumin and serum creatinine testing, because kidney disease can develop without symptoms. A rising creatinine is followed up rather than noted in passing.

chunks.title: Creatinine
chunks.text: Serum creatinine is used as a marker of kidney function, usually alongside an estimated glomerular filtration rate. Values are interpreted against the laboratory's reference range and, more usefully, against the patient's own previous results, since a trend carries more information than a single value.

chunks.title: Documents
chunks.text: A result that arrives only as a scanned document is not visible to the searches and alerts that run over structured records until someone enters it. Until then it can be missed, which is why scanned results are reviewed and transcribed rather than filed unread.

chunks.title: Documents
chunks.text: Information a patient writes on an intake form is self-reported and is treated as a prompt to confirm rather than as a verified record. Medicines and allergies written by a patient are checked against the chart before the chart is changed.
